subject: physics_2
question_text: What is the phenomenon involved in the working of a transformer?

mark_split.label: How the flux links the coils

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: a transformer is two coils coupled only by the core flux; e = −N dφ/dt needs a CHANGING flux, so it works only on a.c. and the coupling between the two circuits is mutual induction, matching the book's answer.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Mutual induction named
lines: Mutual induction is the phenomenon behind
steps.margin_note: First mark. The word mutual must appear.
steps.why: Naming mutual induction is the asked fact — the transformer is two circuits coupled only by magnetic flux, and an emf induced in one coil by a changing current in the other is exactly what mutual induction means.
common_mistakes: Writing self induction. The emf appears in the OTHER coil, so it is mutual induction.
Writing electromagnetic induction alone. Name the mutual kind — the flux of one coil links the other coil.

recall.must_convey: That mutual induction is the phenomenon behind the working of a transformer.
accept: mutual inductance between the two coils

steps.memory_tip: Two coils, so the induction is mutual — self induction needs only one coil.

steps.label: How the flux links the coils
lines: An alternating current in the primary coil
sets up a changing magnetic flux in the core.
This changing flux links the secondary coil
and induces an emf in it.
A transformer therefore works only on a.c.
and does nothing with steady d.c.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. One sentence of mechanism: changing flux in the core, linked to the secondary.
steps.why: The one-line mechanism shows why the name fits: only a CHANGING flux induces an emf, which is also why a transformer needs a.c. and is useless on steady d.c.
common_mistakes: Saying a transformer also works on d.c. A steady current gives a steady flux, and a steady flux induces no emf.

recall.must_convey: That the alternating current in the primary makes a changing flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an emf; steady d.c. induces nothing.

steps.memory_tip: No change, no emf. The flux must keep changing, so the supply must be a.c.

insider_note: The word mutual carries the mark — self induction, or plain induction, is the common wrong answer here.
